6d317f6671a4.t: How the 12 Traditions Came About (1937–1950): The History, From the Sources | Recovery Starts

83ccc289e6bd.t: How and why A.A.'s Twelve Traditions were written: the 1937 lesson, the growing pains of the 1940s, Bill W.'s "Twelve Points to Assure Our Future" (Grapevine, May 1946), the short form, and the Cleveland convention of July 1950. Every claim cited to the Big Book, the Grapevine essays and A.A. Comes of Age.

05a0f927b105.t: How the 12 Traditions Came About (1937–1950): The History, From the Sources

101654e15c04.t: Thirteen years, from a group that told Bill W. no in 1937 to a convention that said yes in 1950. Told only from the sources: the Big Book, Bill W.'s Grapevine essays of 1946–1947, and <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>.

56e9cc5ca019.t: The Twelve Traditions are what A.A.'s groups learned the hard way in their first years, written down so the next group wouldn't have to learn it the same way. The Big Book says they answer two questions: "How can A.A. best function?" and, "How can A.A. best stay whole and so survive?" (p. 561).

e6df6683802e.t: Bill W. put them on paper as "Twelve Points to Assure Our Future," the Long Form, in the A.A. Grapevine of May 1946, and explained them in Grapevine essays through 1946 and 1947. They were cut down to the short form starting around 1947, and A.A.'s first International Convention, in Cleveland in July 1950, confirmed them.

3658adcaca7b.t: <0>1937</0> The New York members talk Bill W. out of becoming a paid therapist. He takes three principles away from that night.

d291ce000087.t: <0>1939–1941</0> A.A. grows from about 800 recovering alcoholics to 8,000 members (Big Book, p. xviii).

fdfc9d809726.t: <0>1945</0> Letters about group quarrels fill the New York office. A friend suggests turning that experience into a set of principles.

4250c2e3acf0.t: <0>May 1946</0> The Long Form, "Twelve Points to Assure Our Future," appears in the A.A. Grapevine.

708c571213b8.t: <0>1946–1947</0> Bill W.'s Grapevine essays explain the points, one problem at a time.

8cd28419ebfa.t: <0>1947 or so</0> Earl T. of Chicago suggests a short form, as short as the Steps.

f9689e9b928b.t: <0>July 1950</0> The First International Convention, in Cleveland, confirms the Twelve Traditions.

e0aff0e80610.t: 1937: the first lesson was a no

0393adaccfa1.t: In 1937 money was tight at Bill and Lois W.'s home at 182 Clinton Street in Brooklyn, with several alcoholics living there (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>). Charlie Towns offered Bill an office at his hospital, "a decent drawing account, and a very healthy slice of the profits" to work there as a lay therapist (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>).

2bfd533387c6.t: Bill had all but said yes. That night, at the meeting in his home, the members heard him out and turned him down. "Don't you realize," one said, "that you can never become a professional?" and "we can't tie this thing up with his hospital or any other" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>).

dec73627d29e.t: "Thus spoke the group conscience," Bill wrote. "The group was right and I was wrong" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>). He counted three principles in that evening: "The common welfare must come first," "A.A. cannot have a class of professional therapists," and "God, speaking in the group conscience, is to be our final authority." A fourth was implied: "Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not govern" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>). Read beside the Long Form, those are the seeds of Traditions One, Two and Eight, nine years before any of it was written down.

1ea734ee63c3.t: The Big Book came out in 1939. By the end of that year about 800 alcoholics were "on their way to recovery," and "By the close of 1941, A.A. numbered 8,000 members" (p. xviii).

d92bbcacce4e.t: The Foreword to the Second Edition calls what came next "a fearsome and exciting adolescent period." Would there be "quarrels over membership, leadership, and money," "strivings for power and prestige," "schisms which would split A.A. apart"? "Soon A.A. was beset by these very problems on every side and in every group" (pp. xviii–xix).

257800b5bd99.t: Membership was one of the fights. The New York office once asked the groups to send in their membership rules, and "They took a great many sheets of paper." Bill's conclusion: "If all of these edicts had been in force everywhere at once it would have been practically impossible for any alcoholic to have ever joined Alcoholics Anonymous" (Bill W., "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", Grapevine, 1946; <0>P-17</0>, p. 12).

cc6ec9482046.t: Looking back, Bill said the early scares, slips and romances, turned out to be survivable. The real dangers were "the desires for power, for domination, for glory, and for money" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>).

3b4087cae338.t: Money was settled one decision at a time. In 1945 the Alcoholic Foundation wrote to John D. Rockefeller, Jr., and the guests of his 1940 dinner that A.A. "would no longer need their financial help." "This meant that we had finally declared for full self-support" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>).

10d633817359.t: Every quarrel seemed to end up in the mail. "It seemed as if every contestant in every group argument wrote us during this confused and exciting period," Bill wrote, and "The basic ideas for the Twelve Traditions of Alcoholics Anonymous came directly out of this vast correspondence" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>).

d8d833e7b1bd.t: In late 1945 "a good A.A. friend," whom Bill doesn't name, suggested putting all that experience into a set of principles (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>). Bill was clear about what such a code could and couldn't be: "A code of traditions could not, of course, ever become rule or law. But it might act as a guide for our Trustees, Headquarters people, and especially for A.A. groups with growing pains" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>).

e4a0f524e563.t: May 1946: "Twelve Points to Assure Our Future"

69935b8cbe68.t: Bill and his helpers at the office did the writing. "The Traditions of Alcoholics Anonymous were first published in the so-called 'long form' in the Grapevine of May, 1946" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>). The title was "An Alcoholics Anonymous Tradition of Relations — Twelve Points to Assure Our Future" (<1>P-17</1>, Foreword, p. 7).

957cdcd5b90f.t: Bill called it "our first attempt to state sound principles of group conduct and public relations," which he was asked to publish, "together with supporting articles, serially" in the Grapevine (<0>P-17</0>, Foreword, p. 6).

c66f83bd161e.t: It opens the way the Big Book still prints it: "Our A.A. experience has taught us that:" Then the first point: "Each member of Alcoholics Anonymous is but a small part of a great whole. A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die" (p. 563). Each point is set down as something experience taught, not as a plan made in advance.

bf7c9f62b4cd.t: Bill never claimed them as his own. "Nobody invented Alcoholics Anonymous. It grew," he wrote, and its lessons were adopted "first as policy and then as tradition" (<0>P-17</0>, Foreword, p. 6). Of the Traditions themselves: "I had merely put them on paper in such a way as to mirror principles which had already been developed in A.A. group experience" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>).

aa05bc62a1da.t: "Additional Grapevine pieces then explained the Traditions in detail. These continued to appear for several months" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>). The pamphlet <1>P-17</1>, <2>A.A. Tradition — How It Developed</2>, reprints a number of them, each with the Tradition it stands behind:

be0adcd0a890.t: "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?" (1946): "Tradition Three grew out of this piece" (<0>P-17</0>, p. 12).

0cb0a4b2d4cf.t: "Money" (1946): "What led up to the writing of Tradition Seven" (<0>P-17</0>, p. 28).

4d90b617b1ae.t: "Anonymity" (1946): one of the first articles on the anonymity Traditions, Eleven and Twelve (<0>P-17</0>, p. 42).

865cffa07c99.t: "Hospitals and A.A." (from "Adequate Hospitalization," 1947) and "Clubs in A.A." (1947): background for Tradition Six (<0>P-17</0>, pp. 16, 18).

9c6682409a42.t: "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects" (1947): dangers "that Traditions Six and Eight recognize" (<0>P-17</0>, p. 24).

48fea697fbb7.t: "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?" (1947): the background to Tradition Nine (<0>P-17</0>, p. 38).

66947c902d5e.t: They are frank about how unsettled things were. "In Alcoholics Anonymous, does money make the mare go or is it the root of all evil? We are in the process of solving that riddle" (Bill W., "Money," 1946; <0>P-17</0>, p. 28). And why would groups keep principles nobody can enforce? "Groups see they would disintegrate if they didn't" (Bill W., "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947; <1>P-17</1>, p. 39).

8be63bd08bbf.t: Not everyone was grateful. "When first published the Traditions got a mixed reception," Bill remembered: a violent reaction "especially in groups that had long lists of 'protective' rules and regulations," and much "apathetic indifference" elsewhere (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>). When he traveled to talk about them, the members "were obviously bored," and one letter asked for his drinking story instead: "But please don't talk any more about those damned Traditions" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>).

a387f4ace38a.t: The short form was the idea of Earl T., founder of the Chicago group, who turned up at Bill's home "One day in 1947, or thereabouts" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>). After "a week of wrestling" they had a first draft "which much resembled the Twelve Traditions as they are today," and after "several months more of consultation and refining, the final draft was ready" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>).

92d0cbd67645.t: The Grapevine then printed the new wording "in every issue," and by the time of Cleveland "the understanding and approval of the Traditions had become general throughout our society" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>). The Big Book still describes the short form as "a condensed version of the original 'long form' A.A. Traditions as first printed in 1946" (p. 561), and prints both: the short form on p. 562, the Long Form on pp. 563–566.

d627e0929c99.t: "In the summer of 1950 we held our first international convention in Cleveland, Ohio. About 3,000 were in attendance" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>). It was Dr. Bob's last appearance (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>).

1b8378213d77.t: Those there sensed that Dr. Bob, and many early members after him, would soon be gone. "In the future we could no longer depend upon the authority and influence of our pioneering people for A.A. unity. Henceforth we would have to rely upon spiritual principles, as set forth in the Twelve Traditions" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>).

381392999ce5.t: Several speakers presented the Traditions. Bill summed them up and asked for approval, and the Convention gave its "unanimous voice of consent." "It was a fine hour in that month of July, 1950" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>).

f60666afa336.t: The Big Book's own account is one sentence: "Though none of these principles had the force of rules or laws, they had become so widely accepted by 1950 that they were confirmed by our first International Conference held at Cleveland" (p. xix).

a12904d4fa5b.t: The Traditions were not handed down. They are the record of what went wrong in groups, written for groups, so A.A. could stay in one piece. That is why they speak to A.A. groups and to A.A. as a whole: in the Big Book's words, they answer how A.A. can "best function" and "best stay whole and so survive" (p. 561). Both forms, word for word, with what each one means: <0>The 12 Traditions, what they actually say</0>.

e6e63c38d31e.t: The month of the first Long Form. Bill's own accounts disagree: <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957) says "the Grapevine of May, 1946"; his <1>A.A.'s Legacy of Service</1> (<2>P-44</2>) says the "Grapevine of April 1946." This page follows <3>A.A. Comes of Age</3>.

23dc1b8d4d34.t: The day in July 1950. Bill gives only "that month of July, 1950" and "the summer of 1950" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>).

923c6df8585c.t: Who the friend was who suggested a code in late 1945. Bill doesn't say.

7c1b2da6cde1.t: When exactly Earl T. came with the short-form idea: "1947, or thereabouts" is as close as Bill gets.

37e16f80fd11.t: Which Grapevine issues the 1946–1947 essays ran in. <0>P-17</0> gives the year only.

e6da19601a83.t: The count at Cleveland. "About 3,000" is Bill's figure (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>).

9cf155ee5e4e.t: Appendix I, "The A.A. Tradition," both forms (pp. 561–566), free from A.A.: <0>aa.org</0>

49c9a2089e28.t: Foreword to the Second Edition (pp. xv–xxi): <0>aa.org</0>

bb9448f70f0b.t: The 12 Traditions of A.A. — What They Actually Say (Long Form, pp. 563–566) | Recovery Starts

17aea54414d3.t: The Twelve Traditions of Alcoholics Anonymous, accurately. Short form pp. 561–562, LONG FORM pp. 563–566. They are governance, not theology — they bind A.A. groups, not individuals. Tradition 3's "no other affiliation" clause exists only in the long form.

2ec1591fcb44.t: The 12 Traditions of A.A. — What They Actually Say (Long Form, pp. 563–566)

175f45495662.t: Adopted in 1950 for one reason: to stop A.A. from being <0>owned</0>. Most of what circulates online is the short form with the important part missing.

6873407e4046.t: Three things get said about the Twelve Traditions constantly, and all three are wrong.

5d3ec77c42e7.t: <0>They are not theology.</0> The Traditions are governance — structural rules about how the Fellowship runs itself so it survives long enough to help people. They have nothing to do with God or a higher power. When Tradition 2 speaks of "a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience," that is 1940s phrasing for a structural idea: <1>the group decides, and no single person is in charge.</1>

4ea9c0f453ac.t: <0>They do not bind you.</0> The Traditions govern A.A. <1>groups</1> and the Fellowship. They are not a rulebook for a member's private life, and they place no constraint on organisations that aren't A.A.

0317a5210bbe.t: <0>And the clause that matters most isn't in the version you were shown.</0> Tradition 3's requirement that a group have <1>"no other affiliation"</1> exists <2>only in the Long Form (pp. 563–566)</2>. It is the clause that says no treatment centre can own an A.A. group — and it is precisely the clause that vanished from the internet.

1cd142d55905.t: Where they came from, 1937–1950, dated and sourced: <0>How the Twelve Traditions came about →</0>

ec3b3a451f53.t: The Twelve Traditions — both forms, in full

680af804fc2d.t: Short form and <0>Long Form</0>, word for word, exactly as they appear in <1>Alcoholics Anonymous</1>, 4th Edition. Most sites publish only the short form. A.A.'s own introduction on page 561 says the long form "is more explicit and of possible historic value" — so it is printed here too, which is what the book itself does.

3cc18a3557ca.t: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity.

8326c9dcdfe7.t: Long form <0>· pp. 563–566 — the one the internet drops</0>

0a41494395b7.t: Each member of Alcoholics Anonymous is but a small part of a great whole. A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die. Hence our common welfare comes first. But individual welfare follows close afterward.

6df7141d77f0.t: <0>In plain terms</0> A.A. survives only if it holds together. That is why unity comes first.

dc090246bee3.t: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not govern.

465c653ab0f5.t: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience.

5a66e7943cb2.t: <0>In plain terms</0> Structural, not theological: the group decides, and no one person is in charge.

8016d84c90ee.t: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking.

8eb976079adb.t: Our membership ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism. Hence we may refuse none who wish to recover. Nor ought A.A. membership ever depend upon money or conformity. Any two or three alcoholics gathered together for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group, provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation.

05f06ed6f210.t: <0>In plain terms</0> The long form is the one that matters here — a group with any other affiliation is not an A.A. group.

92026d428c0e.t: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole.

c086e0b55760.t: With respect to its own affairs, each A.A. group should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience. But when its plans concern the welfare of neighboring groups also, those groups ought to be consulted. And no group, regional committee, or individual should ever take any action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole without conferring with the trustees of the General Service Board. On such issues our common welfare is paramount.

86d1709490ee.t: <0>In plain terms</0> Each group runs its own affairs, except where it would affect other groups or A.A. as a whole.

2701ef6630cb.t: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers.

0c6ff5809ec1.t: Each Alcoholics Anonymous group ought to be a spiritual entity having but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers.

830dc24f2ab9.t: <0>In plain terms</0> One purpose. Not several.

fe8083df1556.t: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our primary purpose.

49de96ed8473.t: Problems of money, property, and authority may easily divert us from our primary spiritual aim. We think, therefore, that any considerable property of genuine use to A.A. should be separately incorporated and managed, thus dividing the material from the spiritual. An A.A. group, as such, should never go into business. Secondary aids to A.A., such as clubs or hospitals which require much property or administration, ought to be incorporated and so set apart that, if necessary, they can be freely discarded by the groups. Hence such facilities ought not to use the A.A. name. Their management should be the sole responsibility of those people who financially support them. For clubs, A.A. managers are usually preferred. But hospitals, as well as other places of recuperation, ought to be well outside A.A.—and medically supervised. While an A.A. group may cooperate with anyone, such cooperation ought never go so far as affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied. An A.A. group can bind itself to no one.

6905187c4eb0.t: <0>In plain terms</0> Cooperation must never become affiliation. An A.A. group can bind itself to no one.

d521439e39b2.t: Every A.A. group ought to be fully self-supporting, declining outside contributions.

6d723dab6c8c.t: The A.A. groups themselves ought to be fully supported by the voluntary contributions of their own members. We think that each group should soon achieve this ideal; that any public solicitation of funds using the name of Alcoholics Anonymous is highly dangerous, whether by groups, clubs, hospitals, or other outside agencies; that acceptance of large gifts from any source, or of contributions carrying any obligation whatever, is unwise. Then too, we view with much concern those A.A. treasuries which continue, beyond prudent reserves, to accumulate funds for no stated A.A. purpose. Experience has often warned us that nothing can so surely destroy our spiritual heritage as futile disputes over property, money, and authority.

38a1fdb37dfc.t: <0>In plain terms</0> Not poverty as a virtue — independence, bought on purpose. A group that owes nothing cannot be steered.

dada81e1f569.t: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers.

4300607abd45.t: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional. We define professionalism as the occupation of counseling alcoholics for fees or hire. But we may employ alcoholics where they are going to perform those services for which we might otherwise have to engage nonalcoholics. Such special services may be well recompensed. But our usual A.A. "12 Step" work is never to be paid for.

a98ec7c55d5a.t: <0>In plain terms</0> Twelfth-Step work is never paid for. Service offices may employ workers.

7d5bdf58780b.t: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve.

5307f52d3f80.t: Each A.A. group needs the least possible organization. Rotating leadership is the best. The small group may elect its secretary, the large group its rotating committee, and the groups of a large metropolitan area their central or intergroup committee, which often employs a full-time secretary. The trustees of the General Service Board are, in effect, our A.A. General Service Committee. They are the custodians of our A.A. Tradition and the receivers of voluntary A.A. contributions by which we maintain our A.A. General Service Office at New York. They are authorized by the groups to handle our over-all public relations and they guarantee the integrity of our principal newspaper, the A.A. Grapevine. All such representatives are to be guided in the spirit of service, for true leaders in A.A. are but trusted and experienced servants of the whole. They derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern. Universal respect is the key to their usefulness.

d60e1e5eb52f.t: <0>In plain terms</0> The least possible organisation. Leaders derive no authority from titles.

3b9727d94285.t: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy.

f82b3a38d772.t: No A.A. group or member should ever, in such a way as to implicate A.A., express any opinion on outside controversial issues—particularly those of politics, alcohol reform, or sectarian religion. The Alcoholics Anonymous groups oppose no one. Concerning such matters they can express no views whatever.

202d61fa2a92.t: <0>In plain terms</0> A.A. takes no position on outside controversies, so its name is never dragged into them.

089a17d0f84b.t: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films.

de7b404507cb.t: Our relations with the general public should be characterized by personal anonymity. We think A.A. ought to avoid sensational advertising. Our names and pictures as A.A. members ought not be broadcast, filmed, or publicly printed. Our public relations should be guided by the principle of attraction rather than promotion. There is never need to praise ourselves. We feel it better to let our friends recommend us.

00f1aa0bd3ae.t: <0>In plain terms</0> This governs how A.A. presents itself. It is not a rule for organisations that aren't A.A.

ca8b3e549334.t: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities.

b2076a23b5ae.t: And finally, we of Alcoholics Anonymous believe that the principle of anonymity has an immense spiritual significance. It reminds us that we are to place principles before personalities; that we are actually to practice a genuine humility. This to the end that our great blessings may never spoil us; that we shall forever live in thankful contemplation of Him who presides over us all.

224f284439dd.t: <0>In plain terms</0> Principles before personalities — a discipline of humility, not a gag order.

c316665a1305.t: Where are the Twelve Traditions in the Big Book?

ca86a4499399.t: The SHORT FORM of the Twelve Traditions is on pages 561–562 of Alcoholics Anonymous, 4th Edition. The LONG FORM — the fuller, original wording — is on pages 563–566. The Twelve Concepts follow on pages 574–575. Almost every version circulating online quotes only the short form, which is why so much of what people are told about the Traditions is incomplete.

529845f5621f.t: Are the Twelve Traditions about God or a higher power?

c16e7dad07bc.t: No. This is the single most distorted point about the Traditions. The Twelve Traditions are governance, organizational, and structural principles — they are about how the Fellowship runs itself so that it survives long enough to help people. They have nothing to do with God or a higher power. The Big Book covers personal recovery; the Traditions cover how A.A. governs itself. The 1930s-40s phrasing in Tradition 2 — "a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience" — is period language chosen to make a structural principle palatable, not a theological claim. "Group conscience" means the collective decision of the group, not divine guidance. "Loving God" in that sentence means that no single human being is in charge.

e25e966d64cb.t: Do the Twelve Traditions apply to individual members?

d5129591e0d4.t: No. The Traditions bind A.A. GROUPS and the Fellowship as a whole — their internal life and how A.A. relates to the world. They do not govern an individual member's private or outside life, and they do not bind independent, non-A.A. organisations. They were adopted in 1950 to keep A.A. from being owned, co-opted, or torn apart by disputes over money, property and authority. They are not a rulebook for a member's personal life.

5ed9fec4645a.t: Can a treatment centre or rehab run an A.A. group?

6f0511af8db9.t: Not and have it still be an A.A. group. The LONG FORM of Tradition 3 (page 563 of the 4th Edition) says that any two or three alcoholics gathered together for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group, "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation." That clause is decisive — and it exists ONLY in the long form, which is why it is missing from most of what circulates online. The moment a group carries a facility's affiliation, it is that facility's programme wearing A.A.'s name, not an A.A. group. Tradition 6 reinforces it: an A.A. group can bind itself to no one, and cooperation must never become affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied.

edc09467b35d.t: Do you need permission from anyone to start an A.A. meeting?

3d4cb7d87e7f.t: No. Under the long form of Tradition 3, any two or three alcoholics gathered together for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group, provided that as a group they have no other affiliation. No treatment centre's approval is required. No facility, organisation, or institution can own or authorise an A.A. group. Any alcoholic can start a meeting anywhere with two or three people, and it is a legitimate A.A. group.

409637fe6f94.t: Does “attraction rather than promotion” mean a recovery business cannot advertise?

2c80c0e66df0.t: No — and this is a common and consequential misreading. "Attraction rather than promotion" is Tradition 11, and Tradition 11 is a PUBLIC-RELATIONS principle for the A.A. Fellowship and its members acting as A.A. members. It governs how A.A. presents itself. It does not bind independent, non-A.A. organisations, and it is not a general prohibition on marketing. Stretching the Traditions to bind individuals in their outside lives, or to bind outside businesses, is one of the most pervasive distortions on the internet. The Traditions govern A.A.; they do not govern everyone who happens to be talking about recovery.

640fe9145df1.t: What is the difference between the short form and the long form of the Traditions?

5a855c6f028f.t: The short form (pages 561–562) is the condensed version read aloud in meetings. The long form (pages 563–566) is the fuller original statement, and it says considerably more. The clearest example: Tradition 3's requirement that an A.A. group have "no other affiliation" appears only in the long form. That single clause is what prevents a treatment centre or any outside body from owning an A.A. group — and because nearly every online summary reproduces only the short form, that clause has quietly disappeared from the public understanding of A.A. If you only ever read one version, read the long one.

255a35061044.t: Why were the Twelve Traditions written?

530b8d321fd9.t: They were adopted in 1950, out of hard experience, to keep A.A. from being owned, co-opted, or destroyed from the inside. Early A.A. came close to being bankrolled, branded, professionalised and fought over. The Traditions are the scar tissue from those near-misses — a constitution written to make sure no benefactor, no institution, and no faction could ever take the Fellowship over. The long form of Tradition 7 puts the danger plainly: nothing can so surely destroy A.A.'s spiritual heritage as futile disputes over property, money, and authority.

ae9b95209204.t: Can an A.A. group accept outside contributions or donations?

2c75125bc832.t: No. Tradition 7 states that every A.A. group ought to be fully self-supporting, declining outside contributions. The long form (pages 563–566) goes further: groups should be supported by the voluntary contributions of their own members; any public solicitation of funds using the A.A. name is highly dangerous; and the acceptance of large gifts from any source, or of contributions carrying any obligation whatever, is unwise. It also warns against treasuries that accumulate funds beyond a prudent reserve for no stated A.A. purpose. The point is not poverty — it is independence. A group that owes nothing to anyone cannot be steered by anyone.

63db01761edf.t: Not in the sense of commandments handed down by an authority — A.A. has no such authority, and Tradition 9 says A.A. as such ought never be organised. The Traditions are the Fellowship's accumulated experience of what keeps it alive, written in the language of "we have found" rather than "you must." But they are not merely suggestions either: they are the structural conditions under which A.A. remains A.A. A group that ignores them does not get punished. It simply stops being an A.A. group.

d5dd36656244.t: What are the Twelve Concepts and where are they?

4d751625b4bb.t: The Twelve Concepts for World Service are on pages 574–575 of Alcoholics Anonymous, 4th Edition, immediately after the Traditions. Where the Traditions govern the life of the groups and the Fellowship, the Concepts govern A.A.'s service structure — how the trustees, the General Service Conference and the service boards relate to one another and to the groups.

438c5c1d74a1.t: Is Recovery Starts an A.A. group, and do the Traditions bind it?

ff37af9beca2.t: No, and no. Recovery Starts is an independent recovery-awareness project. It is not an A.A. group, it is not affiliated with Alcoholics Anonymous World Services, and it does not speak for A.A. The Twelve Traditions bind A.A. groups and the Fellowship — they place no constraint on an outside project's operations. We publish the Traditions in full, unaltered and attributed, because the accurate version is worth protecting and almost nobody else prints the long form. That is the whole reason this page exists.
